subject: Anthropology
title: Skin Color and Adaptation
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Skin Color and Adaptation.

hook.text: Dark skin near the equator, light skin near the poles. It's not race — it's a map of ultraviolet radiation.

buildup.text: Skin color is an adaptation to UV intensity. Melanin protects against UV damage but blocks vitamin D production.

discovery.text: Near the equator, dark skin prevents folate destruction. At higher latitudes, lighter skin allows enough vitamin D.

twist.text: Skin color has changed multiple times in human history. It's one of the fastest-evolving and simplest adaptations.

climax.text: Skin color is biology adapting to sunlight — nothing more. It carries no information about intelligence or ability.

punchline.text: Skin color is a sunlight adaptation, not a category.

quiz.question: What determines human skin color variation?

details.summary: Human skin color variation is an adaptation to different UV radiation levels. Dark skin near the equator protects folate from UV destruction. Lighter skin at higher latitudes allows sufficient vitamin D synthesis from weaker sunlight.
details.whyItMatters: Skin color is the most visible human variation and the primary basis for racial classification. Showing it is a simple environmental adaptation demolishes the idea that it signals deeper biological differences between human groups.
takeaways: Skin color is an adaptation to UV radiation levels by latitude
Dark skin protects folate; light skin enables vitamin D synthesis
It is a superficial environmental adaptation, not a racial marker

faq.question: Why does skin color correlate with latitude?
faq.answer: Intense equatorial UV radiation destroys folate, essential for fetal development — dark melanin provides protection. At higher latitudes, weaker UV makes vitamin D synthesis difficult — lighter skin allows more UV penetration. The gradient tracks UV intensity, not racial boundaries.

faq.question: How quickly can skin color evolve?
faq.answer: Relatively quickly by evolutionary standards. Populations moving to new latitudes can evolve significantly different skin pigmentation within several thousand years. European light skin evolved within the last 10,000 years.
